pamphlet_excerpts: Rockfall Protection: Climbers and belayers must wear approved helmets within active crag rockfall zones.
Anchor Redundancy: Multi-point anchors require independent load distribution to survive a single component failure.
Hypothermia Prevention: Wet climbing clothing accelerates rapid core cooling even during warm summer ascents.
Lightning Protocol: High crag exposure requires immediate descent when thunder clouds approach the area.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Perimeter Check: Survey the crag cliff base to identify loose rock and drainage hazards.
Step 2 - Safe Zone Setup: Designate a protected gear staging and resting location outside falling rock zones.
Step 3 - First Aid Prep: Place an accessible first aid kit near the staging ground before climbing.
Step 4 - Hazard Briefing: Review rockfall warning calls, weather retreat routes, and evacuation tasks with partners.

misconception_pool.misconception: Popping a friction blister on your fingers immediately after a climb speeds up skin healing on multi-day trips.
misconception_pool.fact: Intact blister skin forms a sterile barrier against infection; keep it unpopped and protect it with a moleskin doughnut pad.

misconception_pool.misconception: Standing directly beneath the active climber gives the ground crew the best view to spot falling gear or loose rock.

misconception_pool.misconception: Rubbing frostbitten fingers vigorously near a camp stove restores circulation faster after a cold weather climb.
misconception_pool.fact: Rubbing frozen tissue causes severe cellular damage from ice crystals; rewarm frostbitten skin gently in lukewarm water around 100 degrees F.

misconception_pool.misconception: Giving salt tablets and cold caffeinated soda to a dizzy climber rapidly reverses dehydration at a sunny crag.
misconception_pool.fact: High salt concentrations and caffeine worsen cellular dehydration; move the climber to shade and give small sips of cool water or electrolytes.

pamphlet_excerpts: Durable Surfaces: Travel on established trails to preserve sensitive vegetation growing around cliff bases.
Waste Removal: Pack out all athletic tape, food scraps, and solid personal sanitary waste.
Natural State: Leave natural rocks, plants, and historical artifacts undisturbed for other crag visitors.
Respect Wildlife: Avoid disturbing nesting cliff birds during designated springtime nesting restriction periods.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Trail Travel: Walk exclusively along marked trails when approaching the designated rock cliff base.
Step 2 - Staging Placement: Position backpacks and gear on durable flat rocks rather than fragile vegetation.
Step 3 - Chalk Cleanup: Brush excess chalk residue from holds before packing equipment at day end.
Step 4 - Waste Sweep: Collect every stray wrapper, tape scrap, and gear strand before departing.

misconception_pool.misconception: Bright white gymnastics chalk is harmless to rock faces because rain washes every trace off within a single storm.
misconception_pool.fact: White chalk leaves permanent visual scars under overhangs and alters rock pH; use rock-colored chalk sparingly or clean tick marks with a brush.

misconception_pool.misconception: Chipping a small edge into blank rock improves safety without violating Leave No Trace ethics at local crags.
misconception_pool.fact: Altering natural rock permanently destroys the resource for future climbers; climb only using natural features that already exist on the wall.

misconception_pool.misconception: Wrapping nylon webbing directly around a living cliff-edge pine tree for top-rope lowering causes no lasting harm.
misconception_pool.fact: Rope and webbing friction strips cambium bark and girdles trees; pad tree trunks with canvas protectors or use established bolted anchors.

misconception_pool.misconception: Burying fruit peels and biodegradable food scraps under boulders at the cliff base helps enrich poor mountain soil.
misconception_pool.fact: Organic trash rots slowly in rocky microclimates and attracts scavengers to the crag; pack out all food scraps and human waste in WAG bags.

pamphlet_excerpts: Snug Fit: Wear form-fitting athletic layers that cannot catch inside active belay friction hardware.
Hair Restraint: Tie long hair securely back against the head to avoid moving gear.
Jewelry Removal: Remove all rings, necklaces, and wristwatches before touching climbing ropes or hardware.
Weather Shells: Pack breathable, water-resistant outer layers to withstand sudden temperature drops at crags.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Jewelry Removal: Take off all rings, necklaces, bracelets, and watches before putting on gear.
Step 2 - Hair Securing: Fasten long hair tightly behind the neck using a clean elastic band.
Step 3 - Garment Tucking: Tuck loose shirts and waist drawstrings completely inside the climbing harness waistbelt.
Step 4 - Footwear Lacing: Tie climbing shoes securely to prevent foot slippage on small rock edges.

Tying a Webbing Runner: A piece of webbing can be tied into a loop known as a runner with a water knot (p. 49).

misconception_pool.misconception: Climbers can begin ascending as soon as they finish tying their figure eight knot.
misconception_pool.fact: Standard climbing commands must be concise, unambiguous, and acknowledged before taking any physical action.

misconception_pool.misconception: Shouting 'Tension!' and 'Slack!' mean the exact same thing when a climber needs the belayer to tighten the rope.
misconception_pool.fact: 'Tension' or 'Up rope' instructs the belayer to pull in loose rope, whereas 'Slack' tells the belayer to feed out extra rope to the climber.

misconception_pool.misconception: A climber can step off the ground immediately after calling 'Belay on?' without waiting for the belayer's reply.
misconception_pool.fact: The climber must wait for the belayer to confirm 'Belay on' and then reply 'Climb on' after the climber announces 'Climbing' before leaving.

misconception_pool.misconception: Calling 'Off rappel!' tells the fireman's belayer at the bottom of the cliff to pull down smoothly on the brake rope.
misconception_pool.fact: 'Off rappel' announces that the rappeller has disconnected from the rope and cleared the fall zone so the next Scout can begin rigging.

misconception_pool.misconception: Yelling 'Heads up!' is the standard BSA command when a rock or piece of metal hardware falls from high on a climb.
misconception_pool.fact: 'Heads up' causes people below to look upward into the falling object; always shout 'Rock!' so everyone keeps their helmeted head down.

Static Durability: Static ropes provide low-stretch efficiency for rappelling, hauling, and fixed-line rescue operations.
Sheath Inspection: Check the outer rope mantle for cuts, heavy abrasion, and exposed white core.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Visual Sweep: Examine the woven sheath along the entire rope length for fuzzy spots.

Step 3 - Log Review: Check the gear log for severe fall history, chemical exposure, or age.
Step 4 - Butterfly Coiling: Drape uniform loops over shoulders and finish with a secure locking wrap.

pamphlet_excerpts: Dry Environment: Store ropes in well-ventilated dry areas away from damp concrete ground surfaces.
Chemical Isolation: Keep nylon climbing gear away from automotive battery acid and bleach fumes.
Hardware Protection: Hang metal carabiners and belay devices to prevent corrosion and grit accumulation.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Gear Cleaning: Wipe dirt and dried grit from hardware using a clean dry cloth.

Step 3 - Equipment Bagging: Place coiled ropes and harnesses inside breathable canvas gear storage bags.
Step 4 - Shelf Placement: Store gear bags on elevated shelves away from direct sun and chemicals.
